trial_name: PANTER — Step-up Approach vs Open Necrosectomy in Necrotizing Pancreatitis (2010)
citation: van Santvoort HC, Besselink MG, Bakker OJ, Hofker HS, Boermeester MA, Dejong CH, et al. A step-up approach or open necrosectomy for necrotizing pancreatitis. N Engl J Med. 2010;362(16):1491-1502
one_liner: The step-up approach reduced major complications or death from 69% to 40% (RR 0.57, p=0.006) in infected necrotizing pancreatitis, driven by fewer new organ failures, with no mortality difference.

pico.population: Adult patients with (suspected) infected necrotizing pancreatitis requiring invasive intervention, median 30 days from symptom onset, APACHE II ~15, in tertiary care ICUs.
pico.intervention: Step-up strategy: initial percutaneous catheter drainage (preferably retroperitoneal) or endoscopic drainage, reassessed at 72h; escalation to additional drainage then minimally invasive necrosectomy (VARD) only if persistent sepsis/deterioration.
pico.comparison: Primary open necrosectomy via laparotomy with standardised technique and continuous post-operative lavage.
pico.outcome: Composite of major complications (new-onset multiple-organ failure or systemic complications, perforation/fistula, bleeding requiring intervention) or death, during admission and up to 3 months after discharge.

background.existing_knowledge: Infected pancreatic necrosis was traditionally managed with open necrosectomy, which carries high morbidity including new organ failure, fistulas, bleeding, and prolonged ICU stays.
background.knowledge_gap: Limited comparative evidence existed for minimally invasive step-up strategies versus primary open necrosectomy.
background.hypothesis: That a protocolised step-up strategy (drain first, minimally invasive necrosectomy only if needed) reduces major complications and/or death compared with primary open necrosectomy.

methods.design: Multicentre, randomised, parallel-group trial. Unblinded intervention delivery with blinded endpoint adjudication.
methods.setting: Tertiary centres with interventional radiology and pancreatic surgery expertise.

inclusion: Adults with acute pancreatitis and pancreatic/peripancreatic necrosis
Confirmed or suspected infected necrosis (positive culture, gas on CT, or persistent sepsis with clinical deterioration)
Decision that invasive intervention was indicated
exclusion: Prior laparotomy for the current pancreatitis episode
Acute intra-abdominal complications requiring urgent laparotomy (visceral perforation, active bleeding, abdominal compartment syndrome)

methods.intervention: Initial percutaneous catheter drainage (preferably retroperitoneal) or endoscopic drainage (14Fr median, upsized if needed), reassessed at 72h; if inadequate improvement, additional drainage; if persistent deterioration, VARD necrosectomy. Post-necrosectomy lavage ≥10 L/24h.
methods.comparison: Primary open necrosectomy via laparotomy with standardised technique, continuous post-operative lavage ≥10 L/24h; additional laparotomies permitted for persistent sepsis.
methods.blinding: Treating teams and patients unblinded; an adjudication committee assessed endpoints blinded to treatment allocation; CT images reviewed blinded.
methods.sample_size_power: Power calculation assumed reduction in primary composite from 45% to 16% (absolute 29%), 80% power, two-sided alpha 0.05; required n=88.
methods.primary_outcome: Composite of major complications (new-onset multiple-organ failure, systemic complications, perforation/fistula, bleeding requiring intervention) or death, during admission and up to 3 months after discharge.
secondary_outcomes: New ICU admission after first intervention
Late morbidity (incisional hernia, new-onset diabetes, pancreatic enzyme use)

headline_bullets: Primary composite (major complications or death) 40% step-up vs 69% open (RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.38–0.87; p=0.006)
New-onset multiple-organ failure/systemic complications 12% vs 42% (RR 0.28, 95% CI 0.11–0.67; p=0.001)

Step-up avoided necrosectomy in 40% of patients and reduced incisional hernia (7% vs 24%), new-onset diabetes (16% vs 38%), and pancreatic enzyme use (7% vs 33%), with lower costs (€90,086 vs €122,268)

outcomes_table.outcome: Primary composite: major complications or death
outcomes_table.note: Composite: new-onset MOF, systemic complications, perforation/fistula, bleeding requiring intervention, or death

outcomes_table.outcome: New-onset multiple-organ failure or systemic complications
outcomes_table.note: Dominant driver of primary composite reduction

outcomes_table.outcome: Enterocutaneous fistula or perforation requiring intervention
New ICU admission after first intervention

safety: New-onset multiple-organ failure or systemic complications: 12% vs 42%
No unexpected adverse events; overall complication burden lower in step-up group

domains.notes: Centralised, stratified by centre and retroperitoneal access feasibility; baseline characteristics well balanced (APACHE II 14.6 vs 15.0, MOF 35% vs 29%).
Unblinded procedural care, but endpoints adjudicated blinded and CT reviewed blinded, mitigating bias.
All 88 patients analysed by ITT; no loss to follow-up for primary endpoint.

Adherence high; step-up arm: 40/43 had retroperitoneal drainage, 2 endoscopic, 1 transabdominal; 17/43 (40%) avoided necrosectomy; open arm: 44/45 had laparotomy; crossovers minimal (2 step-up patients had laparotomy, 1 open had VARD).
Well matched for severity, comorbidity, and duration of symptoms.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is strong to moderate: allocation and blinded adjudication support credibility, but unblinded care and complex co-interventions pose a residual risk of performance bias, largely buffered by objective outcomes and adjudication.

domains.notes: Severely ill patients with infected necrosis managed in tertiary centres; reflects typical cohort requiring intervention, but excludes those needing urgent laparotomy.
Requires interventional radiology and surgical expertise for VARD/laparotomy; outcomes may differ in centres without established minimally invasive pathways or in earlier disease phases.

external_validity.verdict: Generalisability is moderate: findings apply best to multidisciplinary tertiary pancreatitis services; extrapolation to early intervention or low-resource settings is limited.

strengths: Blinded adjudication of outcomes and blinded CT review
Robust reporting of procedural intensity and downstream morbidity
Incorporation of societal cost analysis over 6 months
limitations: Small sample size with limited power for mortality
Primary endpoint is composite with components of differing clinical weight
Specialised centre expertise and late randomisation (median 30 days) may limit applicability to earlier or less-selected disease trajectories

critical_appraisal.summary: PANTER is a well-conducted, practice-changing RCT that established the step-up paradigm. The large reduction in major complications, especially new organ failure, is clinically important and supported by consistent secondary outcomes. Limitations include small sample size, unblinded delivery, and composite endpoint heterogeneity, but the overall evidence level is high.
strengths: Comprehensive outcome reporting including late morbidity and costs
weaknesses: Composite endpoint components may differ in importance

sections.authors_conclusion: The step-up approach for infected necrotizing pancreatitis significantly reduces major complications and late morbidity compared with open necrosectomy, with no difference in mortality. A protocolised escalation strategy—drain first, debride only if necessary—should be the preferred management in patients suitable for percutaneous drainage.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: PANTER changed practice by demonstrating that a step-up strategy—drain first, debride only if necessary—reduces major complications (especially new organ failure) and late sequelae without increasing mortality, in patients with infected necrotizing pancreatitis requiring intervention.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Patients with (suspected) infected necrotizing pancreatitis in tertiary care settings, particularly those with mature walled-off necrosis (median ~30 days from onset), and without urgent indication for laparotomy.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: It does not mean that mortality is lower with step-up; nor does it imply that earlier open surgery is always harmful. The timing of randomisation was late, and the trial excluded those requiring immediate surgery.
implementation_caveats: Requires experienced interventional radiology for percutaneous drainage
Need surgical capability for VARD/laparotomy if escalation required
Efficacy may differ in earlier disease phases or resource-limited settings

controversies.notes: The benefit was driven mainly by new-onset organ failure/systemic complications, raising debate about the clinical importance of individual components and potential for care-pathway ascertainment bias.
An editorial emphasised that procedural expertise and multidisciplinary pathways are critical; broad adoption should be coupled to appropriate infrastructure, not just a procedure swap.

Subsequent trials (e.g., TENSION) compared endoscopic transluminal step-up with surgical step-up, showing endoscopic step-up as a viable alternative with potentially different fistula/hernia profiles.
The POINTER trial demonstrated that immediate drainage does not improve outcomes and increases procedures, reinforcing PANTER’s principle of delayed escalation.

Earlier RCTs (e.g., Bakker et al.) compared endoscopic vs surgical necrosectomy, informing the evolution of minimally invasive debridement techniques but focusing on different technical questions than the staged step-up concept.
Meta-analyses support fewer external fistulas with endoscopic approaches but highlight heterogeneity in necrosis maturity, timing, and endpoint definitions.

context_related_trials.relation: Compared endoscopic step-up versus surgical step-up in infected necrotizing pancreatitis, building on PANTER’s step-up framework; showed endoscopic step-up reduced pancreatic fistulas and hospital stay without difference in mortality, supporting an alternative less invasive approach.

Randomised immediate versus postponed catheter drainage for infected necrosis; found that immediate drainage did not improve outcomes and increased procedures, supporting PANTER’s delayed escalation philosophy.

context_related_trials.trial: Bakker et al. (2012) Endoscopic vs Surgical Necrosectomy
context_related_trials.relation: Pilot RCT comparing endoscopic transgastric necrosectomy with surgical necrosectomy, demonstrating feasibility of endoscopic direct necrosectomy and informing the subsequent step-up strategy evolution.

unresolved_questions: Which specific component(s) of the step-up bundle (timing, drainage technique, access route, VARD) most significantly affect outcomes?
Optimal timing of initial drainage in infected necrosis (addressed by POINTER but may vary with necrosis maturity).
Long-term pancreatic function and quality of life beyond 6 months.
Applicability to patients with very early, rapidly progressive infection requiring earlier intervention.
Comparison with endoscopic-only step-up pathways (addressed by TENSION).

numbers_to_remember: Primary composite: 40% step-up vs 69% open (RR 0.57, p=0.006)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: For infected necrotizing pancreatitis, a step-up approach (percutaneous drainage then necrosectomy only if necessary) cuts major complications in half compared with open surgery, without affecting mortality, and should be standard practice.
